transcript: Adam Gwon's new musical All the World's a Stage is set in the 90s but perfectly meets this moment in 2025. It follows Ricky, a gay high school teacher in a small town who connects with an outcast student named Sam over their mutual love for the theater. When he agrees to help her prepare for a monologue competition, this causes controversy in the deeply religious community that doesn't condone the “lifestyles” portrayed in some of the material that Ricky introduces to Sam. This musical is timely and poignant and very well written. The orchestrations and melodies as well as the whole 90s vibe reminded me of Kimberly Akimbo, and the vocal arrangements reminded me of Dear Evan Hansen. The script is funny and while it moves quickly, the plot points feel realistic enough to hit emotionally, especially at the end. And with a small cast of four, every character gets to develop in a meaningful way. The production itself is small in general, featuring an on-stage band of four and a simple production design which reflects how the story takes place in a simpler time and a charmingly small world. But a small production can have a big impact, and these performances certainly help with that. Matt Rodin is wonderful as Ricky and the entire cast is outstanding, especially in their vocals. Overall, we're not reinventing the wheel here, but the script and the music are great, as are the performances in the direction. High quality never goes out of style, and this is it. All the World’s a Stage is running through May 10th at Theater Row, and needless to say, it has my recommendation. With that, another Playbill for my collection.
